text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Berlin court accuses Iranian leadership of ordering political killings in Berlin. Bonn calls off policy of "critical dialogue" with Tehran.
- Germany's supreme court upholds complex voting laws that assured Chancellor Helmut Kohl a working government majority in 1994 and helped ex-communists win seats in the Bonn parliament.
- Liberal Free Democrats, junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition, launch a bill to set quotas on the number of foreigners allowed into the country.
- States want electricity companies to pay five billion marks towards costs of long-term storage of nuclear waste.
HANDELSBLATT
- Bonn breaks off policy of critical dialogue and European Union countries call back ambassadors to Tehran after Berlin court decision.
- Volkswagen AG launches product offensive, but sees a stagnation in 1997 in the European car market.

- Portugese newspaper Publico reports that European Commission does not think Germany can make the three percent government deficit to gross domestic product target required for participation in European monetary union.
- Proposal by German union leader Klaus Zwickel to create jobs by cutting the length of the working week sparks fierce debate.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Supreme court's decision to uphold electoral law was narrow.
- State finance ministers want German power companies to pay up to four billion marks in back taxes.
- Interior Minister Manfred Kanther says Germany does not need immigration law.
- Skilled crafts association calls for meeting with trade unions over Zwickel proposals.
DIE WELT
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel emphaises readiness to compromise with opposition Social Democrats over tax reform.
- Industry reacts calmly to Berlin court's accusations against Iran.
